book: 218 - The Philosophy of the Coen Brothers

chapters.file: ch17 - “Takin’ ’er Easy for All Us Sinners” Laziness as a Virtue in The Big Lebowski.md
chapters.relation: Douglass and Walls read the Dude's 'principled laziness' as a coherent ethos and test it against the film's rival worldviews: the villains' hollow nihilism (which they distinguish from Nietzsche's will to power and death-of-God), Bunny's Aristippan hedonism versus Epicurus, the Big Lebowski's Nietzschean master-morality egoism, and Walter Sobchak's rules-worship read through Kant's categorical imperative and Locke's social contract. They argue dude-ism works as a personal path to contentment but, lacking any objective standard, cannot condemn true evil like Bunny's threatened murder, exposing its purposeless-universe premise as its real flaw.

chapters.file: ch18 - No Country for Old Men as Moral Philosophy.md
chapters.relation: McFarland reads the film as moral philosophy: Sheriff Bell faces a post-Kantian predicament, able to reconstruct how crimes happen but unable to 'measure' why, and dooms himself by tying duty to an outcome (his promise to make Llewelyn safe) rather than to Kant's unconditional imperative, so failure yields Bernard Williams-style shame. Llewelyn is cast against Kierkegaard's Abraham/Brutus distinction as a tragic hero who cannot suspend the ethical, while Chigurh functions as an ironic anti-philosopher who alternately grounds killing in self-interest ('what good is a rule if it got you here?') and in a perverse Kantian promise-keeping, until Carla Jean restores moral responsibility by refusing his coin toss.

chapters.file: ch19 - Part - 3 Postmodernity, Interpretation, and the Construction of History.md
ch20 - Heidegger and the Problem of Interpretation in Barton Fink.md
chapters.relation: Conard uses Barton Fink as a springboard into Heidegger's theory of interpretation, contrasting it with Cartesian dualism. Barton, the 'life of the mind' artist whose skull-like hotel room symbolizes his isolation, is a Cartesian subject cut off from the practical, meaning-giving contexts (Heidegger's workshop, the ready-to-hand versus present-at-hand typewriter) in which equipment is understood and interpreted. Conard argues the film's uninterpretable elements—the box, the wall photo, the mosquitoes—resist meaning precisely because Barton is severed from the web of relations that would let anything show up as meaningful, illustrating Dasein's temporal, potentiality-driven being.

chapters.file: ch21 - The Past Is Now History and The Hudsucker Proxy.md
chapters.relation: Coughlin argues The Hudsucker Proxy, far from being empty pastiche, is a postmodern meditation on history as a constructed text. Drawing on Linda Hutcheon he treats the film's parody of screwball comedy and Frank Capra as a 'value-problematizing' tool: Norville is a hollowed-out anti-Capra hero, and Moses stopping the clock and addressing the audience foregrounds the artificiality and 'telling' of all narratives. Foucault's claim that resistance uses power's own tools underwrites the reading that recycling dead styles and cultural memory (the J. Edgar Hoover quip, the array of intertexts) challenges the authority and singularity of historical representation.

chapters.file: ch22 - “A Homespun Murder Story” Film Noir and the Problem of Modernity in Fargo.md
chapters.relation: Abrams reads Fargo as a noir study of modernity via MacIntyre's After Virtue: humans are 'story-telling animals,' and the Enlightenment project (Descartes, Sartre) shredded the shared myth, leaving Cartesian monadic selves who float in a void as 'unscripted, anxious stutterers.' The whiteout blizzard becomes an ontological tabula rasa of Heraclitean flux where every conversation collapses (Jerry, Carl, Mike Yanagita, even Marge at the drive-thru). Abrams reads Marge as morally good but intellectually shallow—wrong to call the sublime, Kantian 'dynamically sublime' day 'beautiful'—and Grimsrud as the one who dimly 'sees' the modern abyss, so the film hands the deeper mystery of modernity's crime to the viewer.

chapters.file: ch23 - Part - 4 Existentialism, Alienation, and Despair.md
ch24 - “What Kind of Man Are You ” The Coen Brothers and Existentialist Role Playing.md
chapters.relation: Gaughran argues the Coens presuppose an absurd, valueless world (announced by Blood Simple's 'you're on your own' voice-over) in which characters must, per Sartre's 'existence precedes essence,' invent a self by adopting a style. He surveys the hats of Miller's Crossing, Everett's Dapper Dan dandyism in O Brother read through Camus's The Rebel, and Ed Crane of The Man Who Wasn't There as a Meursault-like figure who forges an identity through violence. Against Camus, murder and suicide are illegitimate revolts, and Sisyphus—not the nihilistic killers—stands as the true absurd hero who never resolves the tension between mind and indifferent world.

chapters.file: ch25 - Being the Barber Kierkegaardian Despair in The Man Who Wasn’t There.md
chapters.relation: Hoffman maps Ed Crane's arc onto Kierkegaard's typology of despair from The Sickness unto Death. Early Ed, the passive barber who defines himself by profession and possessions, embodies despair as a lack of infinitude and possibility—the finitized 'mass man.' Through blackmail, killing Big Dave, and his failed attempt to manage Birdy, he becomes a man of immediacy with reflection, then shifts to 'despair over the eternal,' sensing finite things cannot satisfy. Hoffman concludes Ed ends not free of despair but as Kierkegaard's self of 'inclosing reserve'—withdrawn, watching himself, craving a confidant—having never made the leap of faith that alone escapes despair.

chapters.file: ch26 - Thinking beyond the Failed Community Blood Simple and The Man Who Wasn’t There.md
chapters.relation: Palmer reads Blood Simple and The Man Who Wasn't There as a diptych re-composing James M. Cain's The Postman Always Rings Twice and Double Indemnity, whose core theme is a failed community where self-interest poisons human bonds. Blood Simple dramatizes the Cainian problem—Visser and the others destroyed by instrumentalization and fatal miscommunication—while The Man Who Wasn't There, framed by Camus's The Stranger and Sartre's Nausea, stages its utopian solution. Ed's Sartrean disgust at hair and physicality drives his dry-cleaning scheme; like Meursault he kills and is condemned for the wrong crime, but unlike Cain's solipsistic heroes he ends yearning for communion with Doris beyond the grave, imagining the restoration of the lost community.
